title: Critic supremum attainment is a strong assumption
description: The WGAN derivation assumes the Kantorovich-Rubinstein supremum is attained within the parameterized critic family, which the authors call a pretty strong assumption akin to what is assumed when proving consistency of an estimator.
canonical_description: Kantorovich-Rubinstein supremum assumed to be attained by the critic family

verdict.reasoning: The deep-read paper directly targets the gap's core assumption — whether the parameterized critic attains/approximates the Kantorovich-Rubinstein supremum. It provides concrete theoretical and empirical evidence that WGAN-GP's inner loop fails to capture the optimal critic (normalized Wasserstein estimates off by an order of magnitude, even after long training), and that forcing accurate supremum attainment via the c-transform actually degrades generative quality. This substantially addresses the "is the assumption true in practice" side of the gap and reframes WGAN success as a Lipschitz-regularization effect rather than Wasserstein minimization. However, it does not close the theoretical side: it offers no formal conditions, approximation guarantees, or bounds characterizing when a parameterized critic family can attain the KR supremum, and it does not repair or replace the WGAN derivation that hinges on the assumption. The remaining piece is therefore a rigorous theoretical analysis or a revised derivation that avoids the attainment assumption — still open. Confidence is moderate because the empirical evidence is strong and on-point, but it is confined to specific setups and does not resolve the formal theoretical question the gap originally flagged.

paper.title: Wasserstein GANs Work Because They Fail (to Approximate the Wasserstein Distance)
paper.abstract: Wasserstein GANs are based on the idea of minimising the Wasserstein distance between a real and a generated distribution. We provide an in-depth mathematical analysis of differences between the theoretical setup and the reality of training Wasserstein GANs. In this work, we gather both theoretical and empirical evidence that the WGAN loss is not a meaningful approximation of the Wasserstein distance. Moreover, we argue that the Wasserstein distance is not even a desirable loss function for deep generative models, and conclude that the success of Wasserstein GANs can in truth be attributed to a failure to approximate the Wasserstein distance.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly probes the WGAN modeling assumption that the Kantorovich-Rubinstein supremum (Kantorovich's potential) is attained/well-approximated by the parameterized critic. It shows theoretically and empirically that the WGAN-GP loss is not an accurate approximation of the distributional Wasserstein distance because the inner-loop discriminator fails to capture the optimal critic (e.g., normalized estimates are an order of magnitude off even for static distributions trained for 300K iterations), and that even when the batch supremum is attained accurately (c-transform WGAN), generative quality degrades. It concludes that the critic does not attain the KR supremum in practice and argues this failure — rather than Wasserstein minimization — explains WGAN success, attributing it instead to Lipschitz regularization.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper validates the "strong assumption" criticism empirically and argues the attainment failure is beneficial, but it does not provide a rigorous theoretical treatment of critic-family attainability: there are no formal conditions, convergence/approximation guarantees, or bounds characterizing when a parameterized critic can or cannot attain the KR supremum. Its evidence is empirical and confined to specific setups (static CIFAR-10 pairs, an 8-mode Gaussian, CelebA), and the recommendation is to stop viewing WGANs as Wasserstein minimizers rather than to repair or replace the theoretical derivation that relies on the assumption. A full resolution of the gap would need a formal analysis or a revised WGAN derivation that does not hinge on supremum attainment.
evidence_snippets: We show that the loss function $\loss_G$ fails to approximate the oracle estimator ${W_1^\ast}(p^\ast, p^\theta)$ because the inner loop of Algorithm [REF:alg:WGAN-GP] fails to capture the optimal discriminator (Section [REF:sec:Does WGAN-GP provide a good oracle ?]).
We conclude that $\loss_G(\theta) \approx W^\ast(p^\ast, p^\theta)$ is not achieved in WGAN-GP, so the loss of WGAN-GP is not an accurate approximation of Wasserstein distance.

We show that certain theoretical assumptions on WGANs are not satisfied in practise and infer that aiming for an accurate approximation of the Wasserstein distance with a WGAN loss is counterproductive and leads to worse results.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: The remaining open piece is theoretical, so data collection and compute are not serious obstacles: it can be addressed with existing optimal-transport/duality tools and standard neural-network approximation theory, with only modest experiments if any. The natural feasible move is to avoid literal supremum attainment (which is often impossible in non-compact parameterized families) and instead prove approximation/consistency results for the critic family or derive a revised objective that does not hinge on attainment — a well-defined, publishable theorem rather than a fundamental breakthrough. Tractability is limited mainly by the difficulty of obtaining sharp, general conditions/rates for Lipschitz-constrained critic families and by the risk of the problem sprawling across several formulations.
